Methodology

How DappGo computes its signals

Every label in a DappGo report comes from a fixed rule applied to market data. This page states those rules, with the thresholds, so you can check any reading yourself.

Principles

  • Rules, not opinions. Regime, signal labels, sector temperature and scores are computed by code. The same inputs always give the same output.
  • One published payload per revision. Each report revision is a single data file identified by a hash. Our pages and apps read a pointer to the latest file and accept the data only if its hash matches the pointer.
  • Coverage is stated. Each report says how many of its expected tickers it covers. A report with missing tickers says so.
  • Thresholds are judgment calls. The numbers below are conventional choices. They make readings comparable from day to day. They are not laws of the market.

Market regime

Inputs, all from daily closes: the benchmark (SPY for the US report, the TAIEX for Taiwan), and every tracked ticker.

  • Benchmark trend. Up if the benchmark is more than 2% above its close 20 sessions earlier, down if more than 2% below, otherwise sideways.
  • Volatility band. The standard deviation of the benchmark's last 20 daily returns: calm below 0.8%, high above 1.5%, moderate in between.
  • Breadth. The share of tracked tickers priced above their own 20-day average.

The rule is applied in this order, and the first match wins:

  1. Risk-on if the benchmark is above its 50-day average, breadth is above 55%, and volatility is not high.
  2. Risk-off if the benchmark is below its 200-day average, or breadth is below 30%, or volatility is high.
  3. Neutral if the benchmark trend is sideways and breadth is between 40% and 60%.
  4. Mixed in every other case.

Note the asymmetry: risk-on needs three conditions together, while any one of three is enough for risk-off. The report also publishes the advance-decline ratio and the standard deviation of sector average moves, which describe the day but do not enter the rule.

The four per-ticker signals

Each ticker gets four labels. The apps show them with the reason for each.

Trend

With at least 200 daily bars, the trend is strong-up when price, the 20-day, 60-day and 200-day averages are stacked in that order and the 200-day average is rising, and strong-down for the mirror image. Price above a rising 200-day average is up; price below a falling one is down; anything else is sideways. With shorter histories the same idea is applied to the 120-day, 60-day or 20-day average.

Momentum

From the 14-day RSI and the MACD line: overbought at RSI 70 or more, oversold at 30 or less, bullish when RSI is at least 50 with MACD above zero, bearish when RSI is under 50 with MACD below zero, otherwise neutral.

Volume

The ratio of the session's volume to the five-day average: surge at 2.0 or more, active at 1.5 or more, quiet at 0.5 or less, otherwise normal.

Ownership (US) and institutional flow (Taiwan)

For US tickers the label comes from insider transactions over 30 days and the share of stock held by institutions: accumulating when insiders are net buyers, distributing when they are net sellers, and otherwise a description of how concentrated institutional holding is. For Taiwan tickers it comes from the five-day net position of foreign investors, investment trusts and dealers combined: accumulating above 5,000 lots of net buying, distributing below 5,000 lots of net selling, balanced in between.

How the four are combined

The engine counts supportive readings (an up trend, bullish or oversold momentum, above-normal volume, accumulation) and adverse readings (a down trend, bearish or overbought momentum, distribution). Three or more supportive readings with none adverse gives the strongest label, and three or more adverse readings the weakest. The apps show this summary label alongside the four inputs. This site's archive pages show the inputs and leave the summary label out, because a one-word label reads too much like advice when it is taken out of the app's context.

Sector temperature

Each sector gets points from the average one-day move of its tracked tickers (+2 at +2.0% or more, +1 at +0.5% or more, −1 at −0.5% or less, −2 at −2.0% or less), from their average RSI (+1 at 65 or more, −1 at 35 or less), and, for US sectors, from insider activity (+1 or −1 when buyers and sellers differ by two or more companies). A total of 3 or more is Hot, 1 or 2 is Warm, 0 is Neutral, −1 or −2 is Cool, and −3 or less is Cold.

Mean-reversion screen

A ticker must pass all of these filters:

  • price below its 20-day average;
  • 14-day RSI between 30 and 55;
  • MACD histogram above zero, or stochastic %K above %D;
  • 20-day historical volatility no more than 1.2 times the median of the universe;
  • not already carrying one of the two weakest summary labels.

Survivors are scored and the top three are listed:

score = min(gap below 20-day average in % × 5, 30) + max(0, 50 − |RSI − 45|) × 0.5 + (10 if MACD and stochastic both turned up, else 5) + (10 if volatility is under 0.85 × universe median, else 5)

The score rewards a larger discount to the average, an RSI near 45, agreement between two momentum measures and lower volatility. It ranks matches on one day. It is not a forecast of return.

Options composite score

Candidates are puts and calls with a bid between $1.00 and $7.00. For each one the report computes an annualized yield, the Black-Scholes delta and theta from the contract's implied volatility, and the model probability of expiring out of the money. The composite is:

score = 0.30 × return + 0.25 × safety margin + 0.25 × delta + 0.20 × theta efficiency

  • Return (0 to 100): annualized yield, first multiplied by √(days ÷ 30) for contracts shorter than 30 days, then capped at 200% and rescaled.
  • Safety margin (0 to 100): distance of the strike from the share price, reaching 100 at 10% out of the money.
  • Delta (0 to 100): (1 − |delta|) × 100, so a lower chance of finishing in the money scores higher.
  • Theta efficiency (0 to 100): daily time decay as a fraction of the premium, capped at 100.

The short-dated haircut exists because annualizing a one-day premium multiplies it by 365 and hides the risk of a sharp move. The displayed annualized figure is left untouched so you can see the raw number; only the score is adjusted.

Where the data comes from

Taiwan prices and institutional flows come from exchange and market-data feeds for TWSE-listed companies, and the Taiwan universe is rebuilt from official exchange closing prices and share counts. US fundamentals used in valuation views come from company filings on SEC EDGAR. Option chains come from a brokerage market-data feed. News items in the apps are shown as a headline, the publisher's name and a link to the publisher. Sources can be delayed or wrong, which is why each page carries its generation time and why we publish a corrections policy.
